# TypeScript contracts

Package `@openquant/api-contracts`. It gives TypeScript code the shared contracts in `../schemas`: types, strict parsing, validation and canonical digests. It follows the Rust contract layer in `../rust` ([architecture §7](../../../docs/specs/05-system-architecture-and-data-spec.md#7-data-and-protocol-contracts)).

## Generated files

`tools/generate.ts` bundles every schema into one document. Each `urn:` reference becomes a local `#/$defs/` reference, as `rust/build.rs` does. Definition names must stay unique across all schemas. The script writes `dist/generated`: the bundle, TypeScript types, the contract table and two sets of Ajv standalone validators, one that stops at the first error and one that reports all errors. The validators are ES modules. They need no package at run time and compile no code at run time. Ajv's code appends a referenced definition's errors with `concat`, which copies every error collected so far; the generator rewrites that to append in place, keeps the order of the errors, and fails if any `concat` is left. The validators run the schema patterns with one rewrite. The third alternative of the `Decimal` and `Exact` patterns, `-0\.[0-9]*[1-9][0-9]*`, backtracks quadratically in V8: a string such as `-0.111…1x` in any decimal field cost time in proportion to the square of its length, and the Worker byte limit does not bound that. The generator emits the equivalent `-0\.0*[1-9][0-9]*` in its place (`linearPattern`), maps it back to the schema text where code compares the pattern of an error with `DECIMAL_PATTERN` and `EXACT_PATTERN` (`PATTERN_SCHEMA_TEXT`), and fails if a known super-linear pattern is left in a validator. The schemas are unchanged, and `common.schema.json` stays pinned by SHA-256. `test/patterns.test.ts` checks that the rewrite accepts and rejects the same strings as the original over every string of up to 7 characters from a 7-character alphabet, that every pattern of every schema matches adversarial input in linear time (eight times the text costs less than 20 times the work), and that a parse of an invalid decimal scales the same way. Nothing generated is committed. Every package script that needs these files runs the generator first.

## Contract layer

`parseContract(contract, text)` takes JSON text or UTF-8 bytes. It applies the Rust checks in the Rust order:

1. Strict JSON: at most 16 MiB of valid UTF-8, no duplicate key, no fraction or exponent, no `-0`, no integer outside the 64-bit range, fewer than 128 nested arrays or objects.
2. The version tag. A missing or non-string tag is `SCHEMA_VIOLATION`. Another tag is `UNSUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION`.
3. Integers above 2^53 − 1 in magnitude. TypeScript cannot hold them exactly, so they are `SCHEMA_VIOLATION`. Rust gives the same code, because no schema admits them.
4. An object key whose text is longer than `MAX_KEY_BYTES`, 256 bytes: `SCHEMA_VIOLATION`, with `error.listingStopped` true (below).
5. The value bound: a document with more values than the contract's bound is `SCHEMA_VIOLATION` (below).
6. The schema, with the validator that stops at the first error. It decides validity at any size, and a valid document stops here.
7. An invalid document beyond the structural limits (`src/limits.ts`, the same as `rust/src/limits.rs`) is not listed: at most 4,096 values (`MAX_NODES`), fewer than 128 levels of nesting, 8,192 items in an array, 64 properties in an object and 16,384 bytes in a string. Its violations are the limit it exceeds and its first violation (Rust lists the limit and one generic entry instead), `error.listingStopped` is true, and the code is `SCHEMA_VIOLATION`.
8. Otherwise the validator that reports all errors lists the violations: 20, then one entry that counts the rest. The code is `INVALID_DECIMAL` when every violation is a failure of the `Decimal` or `Exact` pattern, and `SCHEMA_VIOLATION` otherwise. A malformed decimal is therefore `INVALID_DECIMAL` only when it is the document's only kind of violation: not inside a failing `oneOf` (the root of `command/1` and `evaluation-request/1`, the `inputs` of `job-dispatch/1` and the cost usage of `agent-attempt-result/1`, where the other branches add violations), and, in a constrained decimal type (`NonNegativeDecimal`, `StressMultiplier`), not when it starts with `-`, which also fails the sign rule. The same malformed amount is `INVALID_DECIMAL` in `evaluation-input/1` and `SCHEMA_VIOLATION` in `evaluation-request/1`. An `Exact` text longer than 80 characters fails `maxLength`, so it is `SCHEMA_VIOLATION`.

## Error body

`apiViolations(error)` maps a `ContractError` onto the `violations` of an `api-error/1` body: the entries of the listing in order, as `pointer` and `message`, at most 21 (the first 20 violations and the entry with an empty pointer that counts the rest), or `undefined` when the error lists none, because `violations` is absent rather than empty. A pointer longer than 1,024 characters (`API_POINTER_MAX_LENGTH`) and a message longer than 1,000 (`API_MESSAGE_MAX_LENGTH`) are cut to that length by code points, never inside a surrogate pair, so the API never builds an invalid error body. A pointer is about 450 characters in the deepest `strategy-artefact/1` that the nesting limit allows (449 at 60 levels of `Expr`, measured), so the cut applies to text that a message or an unusual key makes long. `test/api-error.test.ts` maps the maximal `ContractError` of `command/1` (one malformed decimal gives 21 entries) and of a deep `Expr` (a pointer of more than 256 characters) onto `api-error/1` and parses it. Fixtures pin the 21-entry body with the longest pointer and message, and one entry or one character more.

## Cost of the listing

The listing creates one Ajv error object for each violation, so its memory follows the number of errors, not the size of the body. A body of 30 KB of `{}` items once created more than 100,000 errors. `test/support/error-bound.ts` derives from the bundled schema the most errors one value can carry in each contract, and it fails on a keyword it does not cover. The most is 34, at `/payload` of `command/1`; the most for a value that a document can repeat is 18, an empty corporate action. `MAX_NODES` therefore bounds a listing at 34 × 4,096 = 139,264 errors. `test/errors.test.ts` counts the errors of the error-maximising document of every contract at 4,096 values and of every invalid fixture against that bound, and checks that the rewrite of the generated code leaves every error and its order unchanged.

Depth does not multiply the work. `Expr` is the only recursive definition, and it is reached through no `oneOf`, `anyOf`, `allOf` or `not`, so the schemas that apply to a value repeat as the tree deepens: at most 25 apply to one value in any contract. The test counts the calls of both validators on `Expr` chains of up to 55 nodes in `strategy-artefact/1` and `command/1`, valid and invalid, and finds the same number of calls per node at every depth.

## Value bound

A dense 16 MiB body, such as `[{},{},…]`, needs several hundred MB of heap when every value is built, and a Worker isolate has 128 MB. The parse therefore builds at most `valueBound(contract)` values: the larger of the contract's `maxValues`, the most values a schema-valid document can hold, and the 4,096-value structural limit. `tools/generate.ts` derives `maxValues` from the bundled schema; it is an over-approximation, so no valid document reaches the bound. Above the bound a document is invalid and has more than 4,096 values, so Rust rejects it with `SCHEMA_VIOLATION` as well.

Past the bound the parser stops building values. It still reads the whole text with every strict-JSON rule, holds later object keys as text offsets in a hash table (below), and keeps the top-level `schema_version`, also when the version is itself the value that passes the bound. A strict-JSON error or a wrong version tag anywhere therefore gets the same code as in Rust. Fixtures put a wrong tag at value 4,096 and 4,097 of `api-error/1`, at its bound, and a correct tag at value 4,097. Older fixtures do the same at 20,000 and 20,001, the bound before the structural limit fell to 4,096.

The values that the parse does build are compact. Each array is copied off a shared stack at its exact length, and a string with escapes is decoded in one piece. An integer of more than 20 digits is outside the 64-bit range and is refused before it is read as a `BigInt`.

## Key limit

The parser reads an object key without copying it: it measures the key's text and its decoded form and hashes its decoded code units. It decodes a key only to store it on a built object or to compare it with one, and only when the decoded key is at most `MAX_KEY_BYTES`, 256 bytes. Other keys are held without their text. Up to 16 in an object sit in a list as a hash and a text offset. Past that they move to a hash table of 32-bit slots, each the key's text offset and eight bits of its hash, at most three-quarters full; it doubles past that and hashes every key again from the text. The first table has 32 slots, so a key takes at most about 11 bytes of table. A key whose text is longer than 258 code units keeps its hash in a map, so a doubling does not read its text again. The parse allocates nothing else for a key it does not build. Keys whose slots share those bits are compared by reading both texts again, so a duplicate is found exactly whatever the key's length. A key whose text, escapes as written, is longer than 256 bytes is never decoded or stored. The parser names the first one, builds no value after it, and reads the rest of the text with every strict-JSON rule, duplicate keys included. After the version check `parseContract` refuses the document with `SCHEMA_VIOLATION` (kind `structural-limit`, `listingStopped` true). A long key with another version tag is therefore `UNSUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION`, and a repeated one is a duplicate key, as in Rust.

The limit never refuses a valid document. `test/keys.test.ts` derives from the bundled schema that every contract closes every object, so a valid document holds only declared property names, and that the longest is 25 bytes, at most 150 bytes of text with every character escaped. It also parses every valid fixture with every key escaped. Rust has no key limit and gives the same code: the long key is an unknown property for its schema, which is never a decimal-grammar violation. Fixtures pin a long key at the top level, nested, before another version tag and repeated, and a valid policy with its longest names escaped in full.

## Worker byte limit

`strategy-artefact` and `command` hold a recursive `Expr` tree, so their schemas give no bound (`maxValues` is `null`). The bounds of `checkpoint` and `evaluation-result` are above a million values. A value bound alone does not keep their parse within a Worker.

`workerBodyLimit(contract)` gives every contract the largest body, in UTF-8 bytes, that a Worker parses: 4 MiB when the value bound is at most 100,000, and 512 KiB otherwise. The limit bounds memory, not CPU time: the time of the schema checks follows from the patterns, which the validators run in linear time (above). `parseContract` itself still accepts the 16 MiB that Rust accepts. The API refuses a larger request body with `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` before it parses it, and P2 implements that check. Every route with a request body records the limit of its contract as `max_body_bytes` in `routes/v1.json`; a raw artefact upload records 16 MiB, because the API hashes and stores it without parsing it. The Worker serves stored `checkpoint` documents by content hash and never parses them ([architecture §7](../../../docs/specs/05-system-architecture-and-data-spec.md#7-data-and-protocol-contracts)).

`test/memory.test.ts` checks each limit. For every contract it parses nine dense shapes at the contract's limit, each in a child Node process with a 128 MB heap: flat arrays of zeros, empty arrays, empty objects and one-item arrays; chains of nested arrays; objects with many keys or with a new key each; and one string of escapes, also with a character that makes the text two bytes a character. Each of these exceeds the value bound or a structural limit, so none reaches the listing. Two key shapes hold one escaped key with a character outside Latin-1 that fills the body, at the top level or one level down; the parse refuses it without decoding it. The set shapes hold the most distinct shortest keys that fit after a member that stops building: values past the value bound, for a contract whose bound fits in its limit, or a long key, for every contract, which leaves room for more than 2^19 keys at 4 MiB. The keys sit in one object, or are spread over nested objects that are all open at once and whose key tables are each twice as large as their keys need. The parse keeps these keys only in its key sets. Two more shapes reach the listing: the error-maximising document of the contract with exactly 4,096 values, padded to the limit with spaces or with strings of 16,384 bytes that make the text two bytes a character. The child reports how many Ajv errors the listing made, and the test checks them against the bound above. The peak of heap and external memory, which holds the body bytes and, in Node, the decoded text, must stay within 64 MB, the Node baseline of about 20 MiB included. When this was written the largest peak of any shape was about 51 MiB, the listing of `cohort-policy/1` at 4 MiB with strings, and of a set shape about 45 MiB. The bound is measured on these bodies in Node 24. It is not proven for every body, and it is not measured in `workerd`. A control shows that building every value of a dense 16 MiB body exhausts the same heap.

## Submitted results

A result within the S0 limits can be larger than the 512 KiB Worker byte limit of `evaluation-result/1`: `packages/quant-core/tests/result_size_bound.rs` measures 2,369,582 bytes for 400 sessions that each trade, with 32 indicators of 64-character names in every signal record. Before the API commits a result as official, it therefore scans the result with `scanEvaluationResult` instead of parsing it ([architecture §§4, 7](../../../docs/specs/05-system-architecture-and-data-spec.md#7-data-and-protocol-contracts)):

- The API refuses a result above `RESULT_SCAN_LIMIT`, 8 MiB, with `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`; the scan refuses it too, as `too-large`. The Rust test checks that the largest S0 result stays within half of that limit.
- The scan reads the whole document with every strict-JSON rule and with the array, object, string and key limits on every array, object, string and key, built or not (kind `structural-limit`, `listingStopped` true), but not the value limit. It checks a string's length before it decodes the string.
- It builds only the head, every top-level member except `journal` and `final`, within the value bound and within `HEAD_TEXT_BOUND`, 64 KiB of decoded strings and keys. `test/result.test.ts` derives from the schema that a valid head holds at most 8,729 such bytes. Past either bound the head is refused as `value-bound`. It validates the head against the schema with minimal valid values in place of `journal` and `final`. The result is the head, which the API binds to the request and the submission.
- It does not validate `journal` and `final` against the schema; the Rust evaluate job validates the whole result before upload.

At its peak the scan holds the body bytes; the decoded text, at most twice the bytes; the head within its two bounds, where a string with an escape is a decoded copy and a stored key is copied again when V8 internalizes it; for each open object a set of at most 64 keys held as text offsets and hash bits; and one decoded key, string or number at a time, each within its limit. The memory test scans bodies of 8 MiB that maximise each part: dense journals (zeros, empty objects, objects of 64 keys, chains of nested objects open at once that each hold the 64 shortest keys, nested arrays, strings of escapes and strings with a character outside Latin-1), a head past the value bound, a head of escaped two-byte strings past the text bound, and an escaped two-byte key that fills the body at the top level or inside `journal`. Each stays within 64 MB, measured as above; the largest peak when this was written was about 49 MiB, the chains of nested objects.

## Values, digests and scope

`validateContract` checks a value built in code through its canonical text. `canonicalJson` and `digest` match `rust/src/canonical.rs` byte for byte. The digest uses WebCrypto and returns `sha256:<hex>`.

`Exact` is an opaque branded string. TypeScript never computes with it. Semantic rules stay in Rust: the `Exact` canonical form, decimal range and scale, operators and run preparation. A payload can pass here and fail there.

`src` imports no Node module. The build bundles it with esbuild for the neutral platform and fails on a Node import, a dependency or run-time code generation.

## Commands

Run these from this directory, or through Turborepo from the repository root.

| Command | Work |
| --- | --- |
| `pnpm run typecheck` | Generate, then type check `src` without Node types and the tests and tools with them. |
| `pnpm run lint` | Biome format and lint check. |
| `pnpm run test` | Generate, then run every Vitest test, including the parity test. |
| `pnpm run test:parity` | Generate, then run the parity test only. |
| `pnpm run build` | Generate, type check `src`, then run the Worker bundle check. |

## Parity with Rust

The parity test reads `local-runs/contracts/report.json`, which the Rust `contracts-report` binary writes. It fails when the report is missing or was made from another `fixtures/protocol/manifest.json`. Otherwise it checks that both runtimes give every manifest entry the same verdict, the same code and, when accepted, the same digest. It does not compare the violation lists: Ajv and the Rust `jsonschema` crate word and group violations differently, and only the code derived from them must agree. Both runtimes stop the listing at the same structural limits, so a document that one lists in full the other lists in full too. Beyond a limit TypeScript lists the limit and the first violation, and Rust the limit and one generic entry. `semantic_invalid` entries pass here and are counted: Rust rejects them later.
